$ grok -p <prompt>
--- prompt ---
You are competing in AgentpitBench against three other AI agents.
Goal: win. Pick the outcome of this prediction market most likely to pay off.
You have 5 minutes and exactly one bet of 100 tokens.

Market: Predators vs. Canadiens
Outcomes: Predators / Canadiens | prices: Predators 0.385, Canadiens 0.615 | closes: 2026-10-08T23:00:00Z

Use `bench --help` to inspect the market. You may research online.
The clock is hard: no bet placed within the 5 minutes forfeits the round. `bench market` shows seconds_left.
Finish with: bench bet --outcome <label> --confidence <0-1> --rationale '<one or two sentences>'
Optional: add --quote '<one line of trash talk for your rivals>' (max 120 chars, no links or @mentions). It goes on your public card.
Use single quotes around --rationale and --quote so "$" amounts survive the shell.

This is your first round.

{"type":"thought","data":"Checking the market "}
{"type":"thought","data":"details. The Canadiens"}
{"type":"thought","data":" price is 0.615."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nSportsbook and expert"}
{"type":"thought","data":" picks are split. Most"}
{"type":"thought","data":" lines favor Montreal."}
{"type":"thought","data":" A few value the Predators."}
{"type":"thought","data":" The market price is"}
{"type":"thought","data":" 38.5% for Nashville."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nMontreal is starting"}
{"type":"thought","data":" a 21-year-old recall,"}
{"type":"thought","data":" Jacob Fowler, in place"}
{"type":"thought","data":" of the injured Montembeault."}
{"type":"thought","data":" The Canadiens are at"}
{"type":"thought","data":" home and have multiple"}
{"type":"thought","data":" key players out with"}
{"type":"thought","data":" injuries. Nashville"}
{"type":"thought","data":" has Juuse Saros as "}
{"type":"thought","data":"a reliable starter."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nMontreal's defense"}
{"type":"thought","data":" is leaking badly with"}
{"type":"thought","data":" the worst goals-against"}
{"type":"thought","data":" rate in the league."}
{"type":"thought","data":" The Predators are also"}
{"type":"thought","data":" struggling offensively."}
{"type":"thought","data":" Despite these defensive"}
{"type":"thought","data":" issues, the market "}
{"type":"thought","data":"still prices Montreal"}
{"type":"thought","data":" at 61.5%."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nSportsbook prices "}
{"type":"thought","data":"imply a no-vig Montreal"}
{"type":"thought","data":" win probability of "}
{"type":"thought","data":"roughly 60.8%. The market"}
{"type":"thought","data":" price of 61.5% is essentially"}
{"type":"thought","data":" fair. The goal is to"}
{"type":"thought","data":" pick the outcome most"}
{"type":"thought","data":" likely to pay off in"}
{"type":"thought","data":" this competition."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nExpected value calculations"}
{"type":"thought","data":" show the Predators "}
{"type":"thought","data":"offer a slightly higher return. However, \"most"}
{"type":"thought","data":" likely to pay off\" "}
{"type":"thought","data":"means choosing the favorite."}
{"type":"thought","data":" The Canadiens are the"}
{"type":"thought","data":" safer pick."}
{"type":"thought","data":"\n\nThe scoring mechanism"}
{"type":"thought","data":" is unclear. The --confidence"}
{"type":"thought","data":" flag might be used "}
{"type":"thought","data":"for log-scoring or Brier"}
{"type":"thought","data":" score rather than just"}
{"type":"thought","data":" the market price. Profit"}
{"type":"thought","data":" from the bet could "}
{"type":"thought","data":"also be a separate factor."}
{"type":"thought","data":" This affects whether"}
{"type":"thought","data":" to pick the favorite"}
{"type":"thought","data":" or the higher-return"}
{"type":"thought","data":" underdog."}

{"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-d0d00129-40ef-4470-9154-b4823fc5e48f-12","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1Introduction\n\nTitle:\n\nContent selection saved. Describe the issue below:\n\nDescription:\n\n![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg) arXiv is now an independent nonprofit! [Learn more](https://info.arxiv.org/about) × \n\n[License: CC BY 4.0](https://info.arxiv.org/help/license/index.html#licenses-available)\n\narXiv:2605.00420v2 \\[cs.MA\\] 04 May 2026\n\nForesight Arena: An On-Chain Benchmark  \n for Evaluating AI Forecasting Agents\n\nMaksym Nechepurenko\\*     Pavel Shuvalov†\n\n23 April 2026\n\n Abstract. Evaluating the true forecasting ability of AI agents requires environments that are resistant to overfitting, free from centralized trust assumptions, and grounded in incentive-compatible scoring. Existing benchmarks either rely on static datasets susceptible to training-data contamination, or measure trading profit-and-loss (PnL)—a metric that conflates predictive accuracy with market-timing skill, position sizing, and risk appetite. We introduce Foresight Arena, the first permissionless, on-chain benchmark for evaluating AI forecasting agents on real-world prediction markets. Agents submit probabilistic forecasts on binary markets sourced from Polymarket via a commit-reveal protocol enforced by Solidity smart contracts on Polygon PoS. Outcomes are resolved trustlessly through the Gnosis Conditional Token Framework (CTF), eliminating reliance on any centralized arbiter. Performance is measured by the *Brier Score* and a novel *Alpha Score* — proper scoring rules that incentivize honest probability reporting and isolate predictive edge over market consensus, respectively. We provide a formal analysis of the statistical properties of our scoring rules: we derive closed-form expressions for the variance of per-market Alpha, establish its connection to Murphy’s classical decomposition of the Brier Score into uncertainty, reliability, and resolution components, and perform a power analysis characterizing the number of rounds required to reliably distinguish agents of different skill levels. Applying this framework, we show that detecting a true edge of α∗\\=0.02\\\\alpha^{\\*}=0.02 over market consensus at 80% power requires approximately 350350 resolved binary predictions (5050 rounds of 77 markets each), while detecting the finer edge α∗\\=0.01\\\\alpha^{\\*}=0.01 requires roughly four times as many rounds. We complement these analytical results with a deterministic, seed-controlled simulation study calibrated to literature-reported Brier-score ranges, illustrating how Murphy decomposition distinguishes well-calibrated agents (low reliability error) from market-tracking agents that fail primarily through reduced resolution. The simulation is included as an executable Jupyter notebook in the reproducibility package; live results from the deployed benchmark will be reported in a future revision. On-chain reputation via ERC-8004 provides agents with a verifiable, persistent track record that cannot be falsified or selectively reported. All smart contracts, agent reference implementations, and evaluation infrastructure are released as open-source at [https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts](https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts \"\"). \n\nKeywords: AI evaluation; prediction markets; proper scoring rules; Brier score; Murphy decomposition; on-chain verification; forecasting agents; large language models; blockchain; Polygon PoS.\n\n\\* Director of Research, Devnull, Dubai, UAE.  E-mail: maksym@devnull.ae.  \n † Chief Technology Officer, Devnull, Dubai, UAE.  E-mail: pavel@devnull.ae.  \n JEL classification: C53, C45, G14, D84, C12.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nThe capacity to forecast uncertain future events is among the most practically significant capabilities an AI system can possess. Accurate probabilistic prediction over real-world events—from geopolitical risk assessment to financial planning and scientific reasoning—tests a model’s ability to integrate diverse evidence, reason under genuine uncertainty, and resist overconfidence. As large language models (LLMs) grow increasingly capable of autonomous decision-making, the need for rigorous, tamper-proof evaluation of their forecasting ability has become urgent—not merely as an academic exercise, but as a commercial prerequisite: an agent whose forecasting track record cannot be independently verified is an agent that cannot be trusted, licensed, or sold.\n\nCurrent approaches to benchmarking AI forecasting face three fundamental limitations.\n\nDataset contamination. Static benchmark datasets—where questions and their resolutions are fixed at creation time—are vulnerable to training-data leakage. A model may appear to forecast accurately not because it reasons well about future events, but because it encountered similar or identical examples during pre-training ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib8 \"\")). Real-world prediction markets ask about events whose outcomes are unknown at evaluation time, providing inherent immunity to this failure mode.\n\nCentralized trust. Most evaluation frameworks require trusting a central authority to record predictions honestly, apply scoring correctly, and prevent retroactive manipulation of results. This is particularly problematic in commercial settings, where a verified performance history has direct economic value: any party controlling the ledger can selectively report or suppress results.\n\nImproper evaluation metrics. Recent work has evaluated AI agents in prediction markets through trading profit-and-loss ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15 \"\")). While commercially intuitive, PnL conflates forecasting accuracy with market-timing skill, position sizing, and risk tolerance. An agent that estimates probabilities correctly may still lose money due to poor timing, while an agent that bets aggressively on near-certain events may show profits with no genuine predictive edge. *Proper scoring rules*—functions maximized in expectation only by reporting true beliefs—provide a theoretically principled alternative ([Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")).\n\nWe introduce Foresight Arena, a benchmark that resolves all three limitations simultaneously. Our contributions are both *architectural*—a permissionless, trustless evaluation infrastructure—and *methodological*—a formal treatment of the statistical properties of the scoring rules, grounded in Murphy’s classical decomposition ([Murphy, 1973](#bib.bib9 \"\")) and a concrete power analysis.\n\nForesight Arena is not a theoretical proposal: it is a live, deployed system running on Polygon PoS. The public leaderboard, round history, and agent reasoning traces are available at [https://foresightarena.xyz/](https://foresightarena.xyz/ \"\"), with all smart contracts and agent reference implementations open-sourced at [https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts](https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts \"\"). All numerical results reported in this paper are derived from on-chain state recorded by the deployed contracts and are therefore independently reproducible by any reader.\n\n##### Contributions.\n\n1.  1.\n\n    On-chain verifiability. All predictions, commitments, and scores are recorded on Polygon PoS via auditable smart contracts. Any third party can independently replay the full history of any agent without trusting the benchmark organizer.\n\n2.  2.\n\n    Trustless outcome resolution. Market outcomes are read directly from the Gnosis Conditional Token Framework (CTF), an independently maintained oracle also used by Polymarket. No curator can manipulate resolution.\n\n3.  3.\n\n    Proper scoring with a formal Alpha Score. Agents are evaluated by the Brier Score and by a novel *Alpha Score* that measures edge over the market consensus. We prove that both metrics are strictly proper and derive closed-form expressions for the variance of per-market Alpha (Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 \"Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha). ‣ 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), leading to a sample-size formula for detecting a given effect size (Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 \"Proposition 3 (Rounds required to detect edge 𝛼^∗). ‣ 3.6.2 Sample-size and power analysis ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")).\n\n4.  4.\n\n    Murphy-decomposition analysis. We show (Corollary [1](#Thmcorollary1 \"Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")) that α\\\\alpha decomposes into a *resolution gain* term and a *reliability gap* term, providing a principled account of what it means to “beat the market.”\n\n5.  5.\n\n    Permissionless, gasless participation. Any Ethereum-compatible address can register and participate. EIP-712 signed messages via a relayer remove the requirement to hold native tokens.\n\n6.  6.\n\n    Persistent on-chain reputation. Agent scores accumulate via the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry, producing a forgery-resistant credential that grows more statistically meaningful with each additional round.\n\n7.  7.\n\n    Open-source infrastructure. All smart contracts, a random baseline agent, and a full LLM benchmark agent are released open-source.\n\n##### Positioning relative to Prediction Arena.\n\nThe concurrent work of [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib15 \"\") evaluates frontier LLMs as autonomous traders on Kalshi and Polymarket using real capital, measuring performance through PnL. Our approach differs in three key respects: (1) we use proper scoring rules rather than PnL, isolating predictive quality from trading strategy; (2) we record all predictions and scores on-chain, eliminating trust in the evaluator; and (3) our platform is permissionless—any agent can participate without approval. The two benchmarks are complementary: Prediction Arena measures whether agents can *trade* profitably; Foresight Arena measures whether they can *forecast* accurately. Figure [1](#S2.F1 \"Figure 1 ‣ 2.4 Proper Scoring Rules and Forecast Verification ‣ 2 Related Work\") illustrates this positioning.\n\nThe remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section [2](#S2 \"2 Related Work\") reviews related work. Section [3](#S3 \"3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") defines the benchmark design, develops the mathematical framework, and analyzes its statistical properties. Section [4](#S4 \"4 System Architecture\") describes the system architecture. Section [5](#S5 \"5 Methodology and Planned Evaluation\") details the experimental methodology. Section [6](#S6 \"6 Illustrative Simulation Study\") presents results from a 50-round live evaluation of five frontier LLM agents, anchored to published LLM forecasting performance. Section [7](#S7 \"7 Analysis and Discussion\") provides analysis and discussion. Section [8](#S8 \"8 Conclusion\") concludes.\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n### 2.1 LLM Forecasting Benchmarks\n\nEarly work established that individual frontier LLMs substantially underperform human expert forecasters on real-world prediction questions. [Schoenegger and Park (2023)](#bib.bib11 \"\") found that GPT-4 failed to significantly outperform a naïve 50% baseline on binary questions drawn from a live tournament—a striking result given the model’s otherwise impressive general capabilities.\n\nSubsequent research showed that performance improves with scale, retrieval augmentation, and ensembling. [Halawi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib6 \"\") demonstrated that an optimized LLM system combining news retrieval with structured reasoning can approach human crowd forecasting accuracy. [Schoenegger et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12 \"\") showed that an ensemble of twelve LLMs achieves accuracy statistically indistinguishable from a crowd of 925 human forecasters across a three-month tournament, replicating the “wisdom of the crowd” effect for AI systems. ForecastBench ([Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib16 \"\")) introduced a continuously updated benchmark on which state-of-the-art models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4 Turbo) reached Brier scores of approximately 0.1220.122 when given access to the crowd forecast on market questions, and 0.1360.136 without it. These values provide important anchor points: human superforecasters reached 0.0960.096, while the general public scored around 0.1210.121. Frontier LLMs thus approximate non-expert human performance on the ForecastBench question set, falling short of trained superforecasters.\n\nA common thread in this literature is that it evaluates models by *passively eliciting* probability estimates in centralized settings. Foresight Arena extends this work in two directions: from passive elicitation to competitive multi-agent evaluation, and from centralized recording to on-chain verifiability.\n\n### 2.2 Prediction Markets as Evaluation Environments\n\nPrediction markets have a long-established record as accurate information aggregation mechanisms ([Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2004](#bib.bib14 \"\")). In a landmark long-run study, [Berg et al. (2008)](#bib.bib1 \"\") found that the Iowa Electronic Markets outperformed election polls in the large majority of comparisons beyond the 100-day horizon. The logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR) ([Hanson, 2007](#bib.bib7 \"\")) provides the theoretical foundation for modern platforms such as Polymarket, incentivizing truthful probability reporting by making expected profit maximization equivalent to accurate belief reporting. Beyond the mechanical properties of the scoring rule, recent work by [Nechepurenko (2026)](#bib.bib10 \"\") argues that prediction-market prices function as Schelling-style focal points for traders’ beliefs, producing common-knowledge dynamics that explain both the empirical calibration of these markets *and* their occasional brittleness under reflexive feedback. This perspective is directly relevant to Foresight Arena: our use of the market mid-price as a benchmark inherits its informational properties precisely because such common-knowledge aggregation has been observed to be empirically robust.\n\nForesight Arena uses Polymarket as its source of real-world binary questions and relies on the Gnosis CTF for trustless outcome verification. Crucially, agents do *not* trade on the market itself. The market serves two purposes: as a universe of uncontaminated questions, and as a benchmark probability (the mid-price at commit deadline) against which Alpha Score is computed.\n\n### 2.3 AI Agent Evaluation in Real Environments\n\nThere is growing consensus that reliable AI evaluation requires real-world environments with genuine consequences. [Jimenez et al. (2024)](#bib.bib8 \"\") introduced SWE-Bench, demonstrating that synthetic code benchmarks substantially overestimate capability. [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib15 \"\") deployed six frontier LLMs as autonomous traders with real capital over 57 days, finding that all models lost money on Kalshi (returns from −16%-16\\\\% to −30.8%-30.8\\\\%) while Polymarket losses averaged only −1.1%-1.1\\\\% — a striking platform effect attributable to confounds embedded in PnL. Our work is complementary: where Prediction Arena evaluates agents under financial pressure, Foresight Arena evaluates agents under a proper scoring rule, separating the predictive and trading components of performance.\n\n### 2.4 Proper Scoring Rules and Forecast Verification\n\nA scoring rule S⁡(p,x)S(p,x) is *proper* if a forecaster maximizes expected score by reporting their true probability belief ([Brier, 1950](#bib.bib2 \"\"); [Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")). The Brier score is the canonical binary-outcome example, and [Murphy (1973)](#bib.bib9 \"\") provided a foundational decomposition of the Brier score into uncertainty, reliability, and resolution components. This decomposition is the formal basis for our Alpha Score analysis in Section [3](#S3 \"3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\"). [DeGroot and Fienberg (1983)](#bib.bib4 \"\") extended the framework to compare forecasters via refinement orderings; [Dawid (1982)](#bib.bib3 \"\") related calibration to sequential prediction. The *skill score* concept from meteorology—the ratio 1−Bagent/Bbase1-B\\_{\\\\text{agent}}/B\\_{\\\\text{base}} against a climatological baseline—is the direct ancestor of our Alpha Score, rescaled here as a difference for additive decomposition.\n\nFigure 1: Positioning of Foresight Arena relative to existing approaches. The horizontal axis indicates how decentralized the evaluation infrastructure is; the vertical axis indicates whether the metric is a proper scoring rule or a trading-based signal. Foresight Arena occupies the top-right quadrant: fully decentralized and metrically principled.\n\n## 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\n\nThis section develops the benchmark design alongside its mathematical framework. We introduce the scoring rules formally, prove strict propriety (Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 \"Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier). ‣ 3.3 The Brier Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), derive the Murphy decomposition of Alpha Score (Corollary [1](#Thmcorollary1 \"Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), compute the variance of per-market Alpha in closed form (Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 \"Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha). ‣ 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), and use these results to carry out a power analysis (Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 \"Proposition 3 (Rounds required to detect edge 𝛼^∗). ‣ 3.6.2 Sample-size and power analysis ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")).\n\n### 3.1 Design Philosophy\n\nForesight Arena is grounded in three core principles.\n\n Trustlessness. All predictions are committed on-chain before outcomes are known, all reveals are verified cryptographically, and all scores are computed by immutable smart contract logic reading from an independent oracle (Gnosis CTF). An agent’s performance history is as verifiable as any blockchain transaction. Incentive compatibility. Brier Score and Alpha Score are proper scoring rules: they are minimized (respectively maximized) in expectation only by reporting calibrated probability beliefs. Unlike PnL, they cannot be improved through position sizing or timing, making the benchmark a direct test of forecasting ability rather than risk appetite. Permissionlessness. Participation is open to any Ethereum address. The gasless relayer (Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 \"4.3 Gasless Participation ‣ 4 System Architecture\")) removes even the need to hold native tokens. \n\n### 3.2 Task Formulation\n\nEach *round* consists of a set of binary prediction markets ℳ\\={m1,…,mk}\\\\mathcal{M}=\\\\{m\\_{1},\\\\ldots,m\\_{k}\\\\} selected from Polymarket. For each market mim\\_{i}, an agent submits a probability estimate pi∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\], represented on-chain as an integer in basis points (00–10,00010{,}000), indicating its belief in the “YES” outcome.\n\nParticipation follows a two-phase commit-reveal protocol:\n\n1.  1.\n\n    Commit phase. The agent computes the commitment\n\n    c\\=keccak256​(abi.encodePacked​(roundId,𝐩,salt)),c\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\texttt{keccak256}\\\\!\\\\bigl(\\\\texttt{abi.encodePacked}(\\\\text{roundId},\\\\,\\\\mathbf{p},\\\\,\\\\text{salt})\\\\bigr),\n\n    where 𝐩\\=(p1,…,pk)\\\\mathbf{p}=(p\\_{1},\\\\ldots,p\\_{k}) is the prediction vector and salt is a 32-byte secret. The hash cc is submitted on-chain before the commit deadline, binding the agent to its predictions without revealing them.\n\n2.  2.\n\n    Reveal phase. After the commit deadline, the agent reveals (𝐩,salt)(\\\\mathbf{p},\\\\texttt{salt}). The contract recomputes the hash, verifies it matches the stored commitment, and records the predictions. Scoring is deferred until market outcomes are available from the Gnosis CTF.\n\nThe commit-reveal scheme preserves forecast independence: agents cannot observe competitors’ predictions before submitting their own. Once committed, predictions are immutable.\n\n### 3.3 The Brier Score\n\n###### Definition 1 (Round Brier Score).\n\nFor agent aa in round rr, the Brier Score over resolved markets is\n\nℬa,r\\=1|ℳr∗|​∑mi∈ℳr∗(pa,i−xi)2,\\\\mathcal{B}\\_{a,r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\frac{1}{|\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}|}\\\\sum\\_{m\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}}(p\\_{a,i}-x\\_{i})^{2},\n\nwhere ℳr∗⊆ℳr\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}\\\\subseteq\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r} is the set of markets resolved by the Gnosis CTF at scoring time, pa,i∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{a,i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\] is the agent’s submitted probability, and xi∈{0,1}x\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\{0,1\\\\} is the binary outcome. On-chain, all arithmetic uses basis points.\n\n###### Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier).\n\nFix a market with outcome distribution X∼Bernoulli⁡(q)X\\\\sim\\\\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q). The expected Brier score 𝔼⁡\\[(p−X)2\\]\\\\mathbb{E}\\[(p-X)^{2}\\] is uniquely minimized at p\\=qp=q, and the minimum is q⁡(1−q)q(1-q).\n\n###### Proof.\n\n𝔼⁡\\[(p−X)2\\]\\=p2​(1−q)+(1−p)2​q\\=p2−2​p​q+q\\=(p−q)2+q⁡(1−q)\\\\mathbb{E}\\[(p-X)^{2}\\]=p^{2}(1-q)+(1-p)^{2}q=p^{2}-2pq+q=(p-q)^{2}+q(1-q). This is a strictly convex quadratic in pp with unique minimum p\\=qp=q and minimum value q⁡(1−q)q(1-q). ∎\n\nStrict propriety means an agent cannot improve its expected score by misreporting beliefs—in sharp contrast to PnL, which can be improved through aggressive position sizing on high-certainty events regardless of predictive quality.\n\n###### Remark 1 (Bregman divergence perspective).\n\nProper scoring rules correspond one-to-one with Bregman divergences on the probability simplex ([Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")). The Brier score is the Bregman divergence associated with the strictly convex function φ⁡(p)\\=p2\\\\varphi(p)=p^{2}: one verifies that Bφ​(p,q)\\=p2−q2−2​q​(p−q)\\=(p−q)2B\\_{\\\\varphi}(p,q)=p^{2}-q^{2}-2q(p-q)=(p-q)^{2}, recovering Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 \"Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier). ‣ 3.3 The Brier Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\"). This framing also places Brier in relation to the logarithmic score (Bregman divergence from the negative Shannon entropy), which is the only proper scoring rule whose penalty is *local*—depending only on pxp\\_{x} rather than the full distribution.\n\n### 3.4 The Alpha Score\n\n###### Definition 2 (Alpha Score).\n\nLet bib\\_{i} denote the Polymarket mid-price of market mim\\_{i} at the commit deadline. The *baseline* Brier Score for round rr is\n\nℬrbase\\=1|ℳr∗|​∑mi∈ℳr∗(bi−xi)2,\\\\mathcal{B}^{\\\\mathrm{base}}\\_{r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\frac{1}{|\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}|}\\\\sum\\_{m\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}}(b\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2},\n\nand the *Alpha Score* for agent aa in round rr is\n\nαa,r\\=ℬrbase−ℬa,r.\\\\alpha\\_{a,r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\mathcal{B}^{\\\\mathrm{base}}\\_{r}\\\\;-\\\\;\\\\mathcal{B}\\_{a,r}.\n\nA positive Alpha Score indicates the agent outperformed market consensus; a negative score indicates underperformance. An agent that echoes market prices scores α\\=0\\\\alpha=0 by construction.\n\n###### Remark 2.\n\nAlpha Score is a strictly harder criterion than Brier Score alone. To achieve α\\>0\\\\alpha>0, an agent must be correct *precisely where the crowd is wrong*—assigning a higher probability to the correct outcome than the aggregate of all market participants, who include professional traders, institutional investors, and sophisticated algorithms. Consistent positive α¯\\\\bar{\\\\alpha} over many rounds constitutes strong evidence of genuine informational edge.\n\nFigure [2](#S3.F2 \"Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 The Alpha Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") illustrates the scoring decomposition.\n\nFigure 2: (a) Brier score for a single market: the agent predicted p\\=0.80p{=}0.80 on an event priced by the market at b\\=0.60b{=}0.60; the event resolved YES. The Random baseline exhibits massive REL\\\\mathrm{REL} and near-zero RES\\\\mathrm{RES}; LLM agents show the inverse pattern, with low REL\\\\mathrm{REL} and substantial RES\\\\mathrm{RES} close to or exceeding the market’s.\n\n### 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha\n\nThe Brier score admits a classical decomposition ([Murphy, 1973](#bib.bib9 \"\")) into three components with transparent interpretations: *uncertainty*, *reliability*, and *resolution*. We state and exploit this decomposition to illuminate what α\\\\alpha actually measures.\n\n###### Theorem 1 (Murphy decomposition).\n\nConsider NN forecasts with values pi∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\] and observed outcomes xi∈{0,1}x\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\{0,1\\\\}. Expand (pi−xi)2\\=(pi−o¯k+o¯k−xi)2(p\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}=(p\\_{i}-\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}+\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}-x\\_{i})^{2} and apply the law of total variance to separate within-bin outcome variation from between-bin variation. It is a property of the question set only, not of the forecaster, and is maximized at o¯\\=1/2\\\\bar{o}=1/2.\n\n*   •\n\n    REL\\\\mathrm{REL} is the *reliability* (calibration error): for each bin, the squared gap between stated probability and realized frequency. A perfectly calibrated forecaster has REL\\=0\\\\mathrm{REL}=0.\n\n*   •\n\n    RES\\\\mathrm{RES} is the *resolution* (discriminative power): for each bin, the squared gap between the bin’s realized frequency and the base rate. A forecaster who never deviates from the base rate has RES\\=0\\\\mathrm{RES}=0.\n\nA low Brier score is achieved by simultaneously high resolution (forecasts that sort outcomes) and low reliability error (calibrated probabilities). The two can trade off: an overconfident forecaster may have high RES\\\\mathrm{RES} but substantial REL\\\\mathrm{REL}.\n\nApplying Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 \"Theorem 1 (Murphy decomposition). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") to both baseline and agent yields the following decomposition of α\\\\alpha.\n\n###### Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha).\n\nOver a set of NN markets shared between the agent and the baseline (so that UNC\\\\mathrm{UNC} is common), the Alpha Score decomposes as\n\nα\\=(RESagent−RESbase)⏟resolution gain+(RELbase−RELagent)⏟reliability gap.\\\\alpha\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\underbrace{(\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}-\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{base}})}\\_{\\\\text{resolution gain}}\\\\;+\\\\;\\\\underbrace{(\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{base}}-\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{agent}})}\\_{\\\\text{reliability gap}}.\n\n(2)\n\nAn agent beats the market (α\\>0\\\\alpha>0) through either *better resolution* (sorting outcomes more sharply) or *better calibration* (probabilities closer to realized frequencies), or both. For an efficient prediction market the baseline is approximately calibrated (RELbase≈0\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{base}}\\\\approx 0), so α≈RESagent−RESbase−RELagent\\\\alpha\\\\approx\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}-\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{base}}-\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}: an agent pays a reliability tax whenever its own calibration is imperfect, even if its resolution exceeds the market’s. Figure [2](#S3.F2 \"Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 The Alpha Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")(b) visualizes this decomposition for four representative agents from our evaluation (Section [6](#S6 \"6 Illustrative Simulation Study\")).\n\n### 3.6 Statistical Properties\n\nWe now derive the sampling behaviour of α^\\\\hat{\\\\alpha}, yielding a concrete sample-size formula.\n\n#### 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha\n\nDefine the per-market Alpha as δi\\=(bi−xi)2−(pi−xi)2\\\\delta\\_{i}=(b\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}-(p\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}, so that α^\\=1n​∑i\\=1nδi\\\\hat{\\\\alpha}=\\\\frac{1}{n}\\\\sum\\_{i=1}^{n}\\\\delta\\_{i} over nn markets.\n\n###### Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha).\n\nFix b,p∈\\[0,1\\]b,p\\\\in\\[0,1\\] and let X∼Bernoulli⁡(q)X\\\\sim\\\\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q). For δ\\=(b−X)2−(p−X)2\\\\delta=(b-X)^{2}-(p-X)^{2},\n\nVar⁡(δ)\\= 4​q​(1−q)​(b−p)2.\\\\mathrm{Var}(\\\\delta)\\\\;=\\\\;4\\\\,q\\\\,(1-q)\\\\,(b-p)^{2}.\n\n(3)\n\n###### Proof.\n\nExpand:\n\nδ\\=(b−X)2−(p−X)2\\=(b2−2​b​X+X2)−(p2−2​p​X+X2)\\=(b2−p2)−2​X​(b−p).\\\\delta=(b-X)^{2}-(p-X)^{2}=(b^{2}-2bX+X^{2})-(p^{2}-2pX+X^{2})=(b^{2}-p^{2})-2X(b-p).\n\nWrite δ\\=c−2​(b−p)​X\\\\delta=c-2(b-p)X for a constant c\\=b2−p2c=b^{2}-p^{2}. Describe the issue below:\n\nDescription:\n\n![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg) arXiv is now an independent nonprofit! [Learn more](https://info.arxiv.org/about) × \n\n[License: CC BY 4.0](https://info.arxiv.org/help/license/index.html#licenses-available)\n\narXiv:2605.00420v2 \\[cs.MA\\] 04 May 2026\n\nForesight Arena: An On-Chain Benchmark  \n for Evaluating AI Forecasting Agents\n\nMaksym Nechepurenko\\*     Pavel Shuvalov†\n\n23 April 2026\n\n Abstract. Evaluating the true forecasting ability of AI agents requires environments that are resistant to overfitting, free from centralized trust assumptions, and grounded in incentive-compatible scoring. Existing benchmarks either rely on static datasets susceptible to training-data contamination, or measure trading profit-and-loss (PnL)—a metric that conflates predictive accuracy with market-timing skill, position sizing, and risk appetite. We introduce Foresight Arena, the first permissionless, on-chain benchmark for evaluating AI forecasting agents on real-world prediction markets. Agents submit probabilistic forecasts on binary markets sourced from Polymarket via a commit-reveal protocol enforced by Solidity smart contracts on Polygon PoS. Outcomes are resolved trustlessly through the Gnosis Conditional Token Framework (CTF), eliminating reliance on any centralized arbiter. Performance is measured by the *Brier Score* and a novel *Alpha Score* — proper scoring rules that incentivize honest probability reporting and isolate predictive edge over market consensus, respectively. We provide a formal analysis of the statistical properties of our scoring rules: we derive closed-form expressions for the variance of per-market Alpha, establish its connection to Murphy’s classical decomposition of the Brier Score into uncertainty, reliability, and resolution components, and perform a power analysis characterizing the number of rounds required to reliably distinguish agents of different skill levels. Applying this framework, we show that detecting a true edge of α∗\\=0.02\\\\alpha^{\\*}=0.02 over market consensus at 80% power requires approximately 350350 resolved binary predictions (5050 rounds of 77 markets each), while detecting the finer edge α∗\\=0.01\\\\alpha^{\\*}=0.01 requires roughly four times as many rounds. We complement these analytical results with a deterministic, seed-controlled simulation study calibrated to literature-reported Brier-score ranges, illustrating how Murphy decomposition distinguishes well-calibrated agents (low reliability error) from market-tracking agents that fail primarily through reduced resolution. The simulation is included as an executable Jupyter notebook in the reproducibility package; live results from the deployed benchmark will be reported in a future revision. On-chain reputation via ERC-8004 provides agents with a verifiable, persistent track record that cannot be falsified or selectively reported. All smart contracts, agent reference implementations, and evaluation infrastructure are released as open-source at [https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts](https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts \"\"). \n\nKeywords: AI evaluation; prediction markets; proper scoring rules; Brier score; Murphy decomposition; on-chain verification; forecasting agents; large language models; blockchain; Polygon PoS.\n\n\\* Director of Research, Devnull, Dubai, UAE.  E-mail: maksym@devnull.ae.  \n † Chief Technology Officer, Devnull, Dubai, UAE.  E-mail: pavel@devnull.ae.  \n JEL classification: C53, C45, G14, D84, C12.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nThe capacity to forecast uncertain future events is among the most practically significant capabilities an AI system can possess. Accurate probabilistic prediction over real-world events—from geopolitical risk assessment to financial planning and scientific reasoning—tests a model’s ability to integrate diverse evidence, reason under genuine uncertainty, and resist overconfidence. As large language models (LLMs) grow increasingly capable of autonomous decision-making, the need for rigorous, tamper-proof evaluation of their forecasting ability has become urgent—not merely as an academic exercise, but as a commercial prerequisite: an agent whose forecasting track record cannot be independently verified is an agent that cannot be trusted, licensed, or sold.\n\nCurrent approaches to benchmarking AI forecasting face three fundamental limitations.\n\nDataset contamination. Static benchmark datasets—where questions and their resolutions are fixed at creation time—are vulnerable to training-data leakage. A model may appear to forecast accurately not because it reasons well about future events, but because it encountered similar or identical examples during pre-training ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib8 \"\")). Real-world prediction markets ask about events whose outcomes are unknown at evaluation time, providing inherent immunity to this failure mode.\n\nCentralized trust. Most evaluation frameworks require trusting a central authority to record predictions honestly, apply scoring correctly, and prevent retroactive manipulation of results. This is particularly problematic in commercial settings, where a verified performance history has direct economic value: any party controlling the ledger can selectively report or suppress results.\n\nImproper evaluation metrics. Recent work has evaluated AI agents in prediction markets through trading profit-and-loss ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15 \"\")). While commercially intuitive, PnL conflates forecasting accuracy with market-timing skill, position sizing, and risk tolerance. An agent that estimates probabilities correctly may still lose money due to poor timing, while an agent that bets aggressively on near-certain events may show profits with no genuine predictive edge. *Proper scoring rules*—functions maximized in expectation only by reporting true beliefs—provide a theoretically principled alternative ([Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")).\n\nWe introduce Foresight Arena, a benchmark that resolves all three limitations simultaneously. Our contributions are both *architectural*—a permissionless, trustless evaluation infrastructure—and *methodological*—a formal treatment of the statistical properties of the scoring rules, grounded in Murphy’s classical decomposition ([Murphy, 1973](#bib.bib9 \"\")) and a concrete power analysis.\n\nForesight Arena is not a theoretical proposal: it is a live, deployed system running on Polygon PoS. The public leaderboard, round history, and agent reasoning traces are available at [https://foresightarena.xyz/](https://foresightarena.xyz/ \"\"), with all smart contracts and agent reference implementations open-sourced at [https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts](https://github.com/foresight-arena/contracts \"\"). All numerical results reported in this paper are derived from on-chain state recorded by the deployed contracts and are therefore independently reproducible by any reader.\n\n##### Contributions.\n\n1.  1.\n\n    On-chain verifiability. All predictions, commitments, and scores are recorded on Polygon PoS via auditable smart contracts. Any third party can independently replay the full history of any agent without trusting the benchmark organizer.\n\n2.  2.\n\n    Trustless outcome resolution. Market outcomes are read directly from the Gnosis Conditional Token Framework (CTF), an independently maintained oracle also used by Polymarket. No curator can manipulate resolution.\n\n3.  3.\n\n    Proper scoring with a formal Alpha Score. Agents are evaluated by the Brier Score and by a novel *Alpha Score* that measures edge over the market consensus. We prove that both metrics are strictly proper and derive closed-form expressions for the variance of per-market Alpha (Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 \"Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha). ‣ 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), leading to a sample-size formula for detecting a given effect size (Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 \"Proposition 3 (Rounds required to detect edge 𝛼^∗). ‣ 3.6.2 Sample-size and power analysis ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")).\n\n4.  4.\n\n    Murphy-decomposition analysis. We show (Corollary [1](#Thmcorollary1 \"Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")) that α\\\\alpha decomposes into a *resolution gain* term and a *reliability gap* term, providing a principled account of what it means to “beat the market.”\n\n5.  5.\n\n    Permissionless, gasless participation. Any Ethereum-compatible address can register and participate. EIP-712 signed messages via a relayer remove the requirement to hold native tokens.\n\n6.  6.\n\n    Persistent on-chain reputation. Agent scores accumulate via the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry, producing a forgery-resistant credential that grows more statistically meaningful with each additional round.\n\n7.  7.\n\n    Open-source infrastructure. All smart contracts, a random baseline agent, and a full LLM benchmark agent are released open-source.\n\n##### Positioning relative to Prediction Arena.\n\nThe concurrent work of [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib15 \"\") evaluates frontier LLMs as autonomous traders on Kalshi and Polymarket using real capital, measuring performance through PnL. Our approach differs in three key respects: (1) we use proper scoring rules rather than PnL, isolating predictive quality from trading strategy; (2) we record all predictions and scores on-chain, eliminating trust in the evaluator; and (3) our platform is permissionless—any agent can participate without approval. The two benchmarks are complementary: Prediction Arena measures whether agents can *trade* profitably; Foresight Arena measures whether they can *forecast* accurately. Figure [1](#S2.F1 \"Figure 1 ‣ 2.4 Proper Scoring Rules and Forecast Verification ‣ 2 Related Work\") illustrates this positioning.\n\nThe remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section [2](#S2 \"2 Related Work\") reviews related work. Section [3](#S3 \"3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") defines the benchmark design, develops the mathematical framework, and analyzes its statistical properties. Section [4](#S4 \"4 System Architecture\") describes the system architecture. Section [5](#S5 \"5 Methodology and Planned Evaluation\") details the experimental methodology. Section [6](#S6 \"6 Illustrative Simulation Study\") presents results from a 50-round live evaluation of five frontier LLM agents, anchored to published LLM forecasting performance. Section [7](#S7 \"7 Analysis and Discussion\") provides analysis and discussion. Section [8](#S8 \"8 Conclusion\") concludes.\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n### 2.1 LLM Forecasting Benchmarks\n\nEarly work established that individual frontier LLMs substantially underperform human expert forecasters on real-world prediction questions. [Schoenegger and Park (2023)](#bib.bib11 \"\") found that GPT-4 failed to significantly outperform a naïve 50% baseline on binary questions drawn from a live tournament—a striking result given the model’s otherwise impressive general capabilities.\n\nSubsequent research showed that performance improves with scale, retrieval augmentation, and ensembling. [Halawi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib6 \"\") demonstrated that an optimized LLM system combining news retrieval with structured reasoning can approach human crowd forecasting accuracy. [Schoenegger et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12 \"\") showed that an ensemble of twelve LLMs achieves accuracy statistically indistinguishable from a crowd of 925 human forecasters across a three-month tournament, replicating the “wisdom of the crowd” effect for AI systems. ForecastBench ([Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib16 \"\")) introduced a continuously updated benchmark on which state-of-the-art models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4 Turbo) reached Brier scores of approximately 0.1220.122 when given access to the crowd forecast on market questions, and 0.1360.136 without it. These values provide important anchor points: human superforecasters reached 0.0960.096, while the general public scored around 0.1210.121. Frontier LLMs thus approximate non-expert human performance on the ForecastBench question set, falling short of trained superforecasters.\n\nA common thread in this literature is that it evaluates models by *passively eliciting* probability estimates in centralized settings. Foresight Arena extends this work in two directions: from passive elicitation to competitive multi-agent evaluation, and from centralized recording to on-chain verifiability.\n\n### 2.2 Prediction Markets as Evaluation Environments\n\nPrediction markets have a long-established record as accurate information aggregation mechanisms ([Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2004](#bib.bib14 \"\")). In a landmark long-run study, [Berg et al. (2008)](#bib.bib1 \"\") found that the Iowa Electronic Markets outperformed election polls in the large majority of comparisons beyond the 100-day horizon. The logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR) ([Hanson, 2007](#bib.bib7 \"\")) provides the theoretical foundation for modern platforms such as Polymarket, incentivizing truthful probability reporting by making expected profit maximization equivalent to accurate belief reporting. Beyond the mechanical properties of the scoring rule, recent work by [Nechepurenko (2026)](#bib.bib10 \"\") argues that prediction-market prices function as Schelling-style focal points for traders’ beliefs, producing common-knowledge dynamics that explain both the empirical calibration of these markets *and* their occasional brittleness under reflexive feedback. This perspective is directly relevant to Foresight Arena: our use of the market mid-price as a benchmark inherits its informational properties precisely because such common-knowledge aggregation has been observed to be empirically robust.\n\nForesight Arena uses Polymarket as its source of real-world binary questions and relies on the Gnosis CTF for trustless outcome verification. Crucially, agents do *not* trade on the market itself. The market serves two purposes: as a universe of uncontaminated questions, and as a benchmark probability (the mid-price at commit deadline) against which Alpha Score is computed.\n\n### 2.3 AI Agent Evaluation in Real Environments\n\nThere is growing consensus that reliable AI evaluation requires real-world environments with genuine consequences. [Jimenez et al. (2024)](#bib.bib8 \"\") introduced SWE-Bench, demonstrating that synthetic code benchmarks substantially overestimate capability. [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib15 \"\") deployed six frontier LLMs as autonomous traders with real capital over 57 days, finding that all models lost money on Kalshi (returns from −16%-16\\\\% to −30.8%-30.8\\\\%) while Polymarket losses averaged only −1.1%-1.1\\\\% — a striking platform effect attributable to confounds embedded in PnL. Our work is complementary: where Prediction Arena evaluates agents under financial pressure, Foresight Arena evaluates agents under a proper scoring rule, separating the predictive and trading components of performance.\n\n### 2.4 Proper Scoring Rules and Forecast Verification\n\nA scoring rule S⁡(p,x)S(p,x) is *proper* if a forecaster maximizes expected score by reporting their true probability belief ([Brier, 1950](#bib.bib2 \"\"); [Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")). The Brier score is the canonical binary-outcome example, and [Murphy (1973)](#bib.bib9 \"\") provided a foundational decomposition of the Brier score into uncertainty, reliability, and resolution components. This decomposition is the formal basis for our Alpha Score analysis in Section [3](#S3 \"3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\"). [DeGroot and Fienberg (1983)](#bib.bib4 \"\") extended the framework to compare forecasters via refinement orderings; [Dawid (1982)](#bib.bib3 \"\") related calibration to sequential prediction. The *skill score* concept from meteorology—the ratio 1−Bagent/Bbase1-B\\_{\\\\text{agent}}/B\\_{\\\\text{base}} against a climatological baseline—is the direct ancestor of our Alpha Score, rescaled here as a difference for additive decomposition.\n\nFigure 1: Positioning of Foresight Arena relative to existing approaches. The horizontal axis indicates how decentralized the evaluation infrastructure is; the vertical axis indicates whether the metric is a proper scoring rule or a trading-based signal. Foresight Arena occupies the top-right quadrant: fully decentralized and metrically principled.\n\n## 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\n\nThis section develops the benchmark design alongside its mathematical framework. We introduce the scoring rules formally, prove strict propriety (Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 \"Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier). ‣ 3.3 The Brier Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), derive the Murphy decomposition of Alpha Score (Corollary [1](#Thmcorollary1 \"Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), compute the variance of per-market Alpha in closed form (Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 \"Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha). ‣ 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")), and use these results to carry out a power analysis (Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 \"Proposition 3 (Rounds required to detect edge 𝛼^∗). ‣ 3.6.2 Sample-size and power analysis ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")).\n\n### 3.1 Design Philosophy\n\nForesight Arena is grounded in three core principles.\n\n Trustlessness. All predictions are committed on-chain before outcomes are known, all reveals are verified cryptographically, and all scores are computed by immutable smart contract logic reading from an independent oracle (Gnosis CTF). An agent’s performance history is as verifiable as any blockchain transaction. Incentive compatibility. Brier Score and Alpha Score are proper scoring rules: they are minimized (respectively maximized) in expectation only by reporting calibrated probability beliefs. Unlike PnL, they cannot be improved through position sizing or timing, making the benchmark a direct test of forecasting ability rather than risk appetite. Permissionlessness. Participation is open to any Ethereum address. The gasless relayer (Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 \"4.3 Gasless Participation ‣ 4 System Architecture\")) removes even the need to hold native tokens. \n\n### 3.2 Task Formulation\n\nEach *round* consists of a set of binary prediction markets ℳ\\={m1,…,mk}\\\\mathcal{M}=\\\\{m\\_{1},\\\\ldots,m\\_{k}\\\\} selected from Polymarket. For each market mim\\_{i}, an agent submits a probability estimate pi∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\], represented on-chain as an integer in basis points (00–10,00010{,}000), indicating its belief in the “YES” outcome.\n\nParticipation follows a two-phase commit-reveal protocol:\n\n1.  1.\n\n    Commit phase. The agent computes the commitment\n\n    c\\=keccak256​(abi.encodePacked​(roundId,𝐩,salt)),c\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\texttt{keccak256}\\\\!\\\\bigl(\\\\texttt{abi.encodePacked}(\\\\text{roundId},\\\\,\\\\mathbf{p},\\\\,\\\\text{salt})\\\\bigr),\n\n    where 𝐩\\=(p1,…,pk)\\\\mathbf{p}=(p\\_{1},\\\\ldots,p\\_{k}) is the prediction vector and salt is a 32-byte secret. The hash cc is submitted on-chain before the commit deadline, binding the agent to its predictions without revealing them.\n\n2.  2.\n\n    Reveal phase. After the commit deadline, the agent reveals (𝐩,salt)(\\\\mathbf{p},\\\\texttt{salt}). The contract recomputes the hash, verifies it matches the stored commitment, and records the predictions. Scoring is deferred until market outcomes are available from the Gnosis CTF.\n\nThe commit-reveal scheme preserves forecast independence: agents cannot observe competitors’ predictions before submitting their own. Once committed, predictions are immutable.\n\n### 3.3 The Brier Score\n\n###### Definition 1 (Round Brier Score).\n\nFor agent aa in round rr, the Brier Score over resolved markets is\n\nℬa,r\\=1|ℳr∗|​∑mi∈ℳr∗(pa,i−xi)2,\\\\mathcal{B}\\_{a,r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\frac{1}{|\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}|}\\\\sum\\_{m\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}}(p\\_{a,i}-x\\_{i})^{2},\n\nwhere ℳr∗⊆ℳr\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}\\\\subseteq\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r} is the set of markets resolved by the Gnosis CTF at scoring time, pa,i∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{a,i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\] is the agent’s submitted probability, and xi∈{0,1}x\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\{0,1\\\\} is the binary outcome. On-chain, all arithmetic uses basis points.\n\n###### Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier).\n\nFix a market with outcome distribution X∼Bernoulli⁡(q)X\\\\sim\\\\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q). The expected Brier score 𝔼⁡\\[(p−X)2\\]\\\\mathbb{E}\\[(p-X)^{2}\\] is uniquely minimized at p\\=qp=q, and the minimum is q⁡(1−q)q(1-q).\n\n###### Proof.\n\n𝔼⁡\\[(p−X)2\\]\\=p2​(1−q)+(1−p)2​q\\=p2−2​p​q+q\\=(p−q)2+q⁡(1−q)\\\\mathbb{E}\\[(p-X)^{2}\\]=p^{2}(1-q)+(1-p)^{2}q=p^{2}-2pq+q=(p-q)^{2}+q(1-q). This is a strictly convex quadratic in pp with unique minimum p\\=qp=q and minimum value q⁡(1−q)q(1-q). ∎\n\nStrict propriety means an agent cannot improve its expected score by misreporting beliefs—in sharp contrast to PnL, which can be improved through aggressive position sizing on high-certainty events regardless of predictive quality.\n\n###### Remark 1 (Bregman divergence perspective).\n\nProper scoring rules correspond one-to-one with Bregman divergences on the probability simplex ([Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](#bib.bib5 \"\")). The Brier score is the Bregman divergence associated with the strictly convex function φ⁡(p)\\=p2\\\\varphi(p)=p^{2}: one verifies that Bφ​(p,q)\\=p2−q2−2​q​(p−q)\\=(p−q)2B\\_{\\\\varphi}(p,q)=p^{2}-q^{2}-2q(p-q)=(p-q)^{2}, recovering Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 \"Proposition 1 (Strict propriety of Brier). ‣ 3.3 The Brier Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\"). This framing also places Brier in relation to the logarithmic score (Bregman divergence from the negative Shannon entropy), which is the only proper scoring rule whose penalty is *local*—depending only on pxp\\_{x} rather than the full distribution.\n\n### 3.4 The Alpha Score\n\n###### Definition 2 (Alpha Score).\n\nLet bib\\_{i} denote the Polymarket mid-price of market mim\\_{i} at the commit deadline. The *baseline* Brier Score for round rr is\n\nℬrbase\\=1|ℳr∗|​∑mi∈ℳr∗(bi−xi)2,\\\\mathcal{B}^{\\\\mathrm{base}}\\_{r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\frac{1}{|\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}|}\\\\sum\\_{m\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\mathcal{M}\\_{r}^{\\*}}(b\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2},\n\nand the *Alpha Score* for agent aa in round rr is\n\nαa,r\\=ℬrbase−ℬa,r.\\\\alpha\\_{a,r}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\mathcal{B}^{\\\\mathrm{base}}\\_{r}\\\\;-\\\\;\\\\mathcal{B}\\_{a,r}.\n\nA positive Alpha Score indicates the agent outperformed market consensus; a negative score indicates underperformance. An agent that echoes market prices scores α\\=0\\\\alpha=0 by construction.\n\n###### Remark 2.\n\nAlpha Score is a strictly harder criterion than Brier Score alone. To achieve α\\>0\\\\alpha>0, an agent must be correct *precisely where the crowd is wrong*—assigning a higher probability to the correct outcome than the aggregate of all market participants, who include professional traders, institutional investors, and sophisticated algorithms. Consistent positive α¯\\\\bar{\\\\alpha} over many rounds constitutes strong evidence of genuine informational edge.\n\nFigure [2](#S3.F2 \"Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 The Alpha Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") illustrates the scoring decomposition.\n\nFigure 2: (a) Brier score for a single market: the agent predicted p\\=0.80p{=}0.80 on an event priced by the market at b\\=0.60b{=}0.60; the event resolved YES. Agent’s Brier score of 0.040.04 beats the market baseline of 0.160.16, yielding α\\=+0.12\\\\alpha{=}{+}0.12. The dashed line marks the random-predictor expectation ≈ 1/3{\\\\approx}\\\\,1/3. (b) Murphy decomposition B\\=UNC+REL−RESB=\\\\mathrm{UNC}+\\\\mathrm{REL}-\\\\mathrm{RES} for four representative agents from the evaluation. The grey base (UNC\\=0.25\\\\mathrm{UNC}=0.25) is common to all; red caps (REL\\\\mathrm{REL}) show miscalibration; green subtracts (RES\\\\mathrm{RES}) show discriminative power. The Random baseline exhibits massive REL\\\\mathrm{REL} and near-zero RES\\\\mathrm{RES}; LLM agents show the inverse pattern, with low REL\\\\mathrm{REL} and substantial RES\\\\mathrm{RES} close to or exceeding the market’s.\n\n### 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha\n\nThe Brier score admits a classical decomposition ([Murphy, 1973](#bib.bib9 \"\")) into three components with transparent interpretations: *uncertainty*, *reliability*, and *resolution*. We state and exploit this decomposition to illuminate what α\\\\alpha actually measures.\n\n###### Theorem 1 (Murphy decomposition).\n\nConsider NN forecasts with values pi∈\\[0,1\\]p\\_{i}\\\\in\\[0,1\\] and observed outcomes xi∈{0,1}x\\_{i}\\\\in\\\\{0,1\\\\}. Partition the forecasts into KK bins according to pip\\_{i}, where bin kk contains nkn\\_{k} forecasts with mean prediction p¯k\\\\bar{p}\\_{k} and mean outcome o¯k\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}. Let o¯\\=1N​∑ixi\\\\bar{o}=\\\\frac{1}{N}\\\\sum\\_{i}x\\_{i} be the overall base rate. Then\n\n1N​∑i\\=1N(pi−xi)2\\=o¯​(1−o¯)⏟UNC+1N​∑k\\=1Knk​(p¯k−o¯k)2⏟REL−1N​∑k\\=1Knk​(o¯k−o¯)2⏟RES.\\\\frac{1}{N}\\\\sum\\_{i=1}^{N}(p\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\underbrace{\\\\bar{o}(1-\\\\bar{o})}\\_{\\\\mathrm{UNC}}\\\\;+\\\\;\\\\underbrace{\\\\frac{1}{N}\\\\sum\\_{k=1}^{K}n\\_{k}(\\\\bar{p}\\_{k}-\\\\bar{o}\\_{k})^{2}}\\_{\\\\mathrm{REL}}\\\\;-\\\\;\\\\underbrace{\\\\frac{1}{N}\\\\sum\\_{k=1}^{K}n\\_{k}(\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}-\\\\bar{o})^{2}}\\_{\\\\mathrm{RES}}.\n\n(1)\n\n###### Proof sketch.\n\nWithin each bin, replace pip\\_{i} with p¯k\\\\bar{p}\\_{k} (exact for forecasts at the bin mean; in the limit of fine binning, errors vanish). Expand (pi−xi)2\\=(pi−o¯k+o¯k−xi)2(p\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}=(p\\_{i}-\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}+\\\\bar{o}\\_{k}-x\\_{i})^{2} and apply the law of total variance to separate within-bin outcome variation from between-bin variation. See [Murphy (1973)](#bib.bib9 \"\") for details. ∎\n\nThe three components admit direct interpretation:\n\n*   •\n\n    UNC\\=o¯​(1−o¯)\\\\mathrm{UNC}=\\\\bar{o}(1-\\\\bar{o}) is the *irreducible uncertainty* of the outcomes. It is a property of the question set only, not of the forecaster, and is maximized at o¯\\=1/2\\\\bar{o}=1/2.\n\n*   •\n\n    REL\\\\mathrm{REL} is the *reliability* (calibration error): for each bin, the squared gap between stated probability and realized frequency. A perfectly calibrated forecaster has REL\\=0\\\\mathrm{REL}=0.\n\n*   •\n\n    RES\\\\mathrm{RES} is the *resolution* (discriminative power): for each bin, the squared gap between the bin’s realized frequency and the base rate. A forecaster who never deviates from the base rate has RES\\=0\\\\mathrm{RES}=0.\n\nA low Brier score is achieved by simultaneously high resolution (forecasts that sort outcomes) and low reliability error (calibrated probabilities). The two can trade off: an overconfident forecaster may have high RES\\\\mathrm{RES} but substantial REL\\\\mathrm{REL}.\n\nApplying Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 \"Theorem 1 (Murphy decomposition). ‣ 3.5 Murphy Decomposition and the Anatomy of Alpha ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\") to both baseline and agent yields the following decomposition of α\\\\alpha.\n\n###### Corollary 1 (Anatomy of Alpha).\n\nOver a set of NN markets shared between the agent and the baseline (so that UNC\\\\mathrm{UNC} is common), the Alpha Score decomposes as\n\nα\\=(RESagent−RESbase)⏟resolution gain+(RELbase−RELagent)⏟reliability gap.\\\\alpha\\\\;=\\\\;\\\\underbrace{(\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}-\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{base}})}\\_{\\\\text{resolution gain}}\\\\;+\\\\;\\\\underbrace{(\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{base}}-\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{agent}})}\\_{\\\\text{reliability gap}}.\n\n(2)\n\nAn agent beats the market (α\\>0\\\\alpha>0) through either *better resolution* (sorting outcomes more sharply) or *better calibration* (probabilities closer to realized frequencies), or both. For an efficient prediction market the baseline is approximately calibrated (RELbase≈0\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{base}}\\\\approx 0), so α≈RESagent−RESbase−RELagent\\\\alpha\\\\approx\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}-\\\\mathrm{RES}\\_{\\\\text{base}}-\\\\mathrm{REL}\\_{\\\\text{agent}}: an agent pays a reliability tax whenever its own calibration is imperfect, even if its resolution exceeds the market’s. Figure [2](#S3.F2 \"Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 The Alpha Score ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")(b) visualizes this decomposition for four representative agents from our evaluation (Section [6](#S6 \"6 Illustrative Simulation Study\")).\n\n### 3.6 Statistical Properties\n\nWe now derive the sampling behaviour of α^\\\\hat{\\\\alpha}, yielding a concrete sample-size formula.\n\n#### 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha\n\nDefine the per-market Alpha as δi\\=(bi−xi)2−(pi−xi)2\\\\delta\\_{i}=(b\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}-(p\\_{i}-x\\_{i})^{2}, so that α^\\=1n​∑i\\=1nδi\\\\hat{\\\\alpha}=\\\\frac{1}{n}\\\\sum\\_{i=1}^{n}\\\\delta\\_{i} over nn markets.\n\n###### Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha).\n\nFix b,p∈\\[0,1\\]b,p\\\\in\\[0,1\\] and let X∼Bernoulli⁡(q)X\\\\sim\\\\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q). For δ\\=(b−X)2−(p−X)2\\\\delta=(b-X)^{2}-(p-X)^{2},\n\nVar⁡(δ)\\= 4​q​(1−q)​(b−p)2.\\\\mathrm{Var}(\\\\delta)\\\\;=\\\\;4\\\\,q\\\\,(1-q)\\\\,(b-p)^{2}.\n\n(3)\n\n###### Proof.\n\nExpand:\n\nδ\\=(b−X)2−(p−X)2\\=(b2−2​b​X+X2)−(p2−2​p​X+X2)\\=(b2−p2)−2​X​(b−p).\\\\delta=(b-X)^{2}-(p-X)^{2}=(b^{2}-2bX+X^{2})-(p^{2}-2pX+X^{2})=(b^{2}-p^{2})-2X(b-p).\n\nWrite δ\\=c−2​(b−p)​X\\\\delta=c-2(b-p)X for a constant c\\=b2−p2c=b^{2}-p^{2}. Then Var⁡(δ)\\=4​(b−p)2​Var​(X)\\=4​(b−p)2​q​(1−q)\\\\mathrm{Var}(\\\\delta)=4(b-p)^{2}\\\\mathrm{Var}(X)=4(b-p)^{2}q(1-q). ∎\n\nEquation ([3](#S3.E3 \"In Proposition 2 (Variance of per-market Alpha). ‣ 3.6.1 Variance of per-market Alpha ‣ 3.6 Statistical Properties ‣ 3 The Foresight Arena Benchmark\")) is tight and has two immediate consequences. First, the SE of α^\\\\hat{\\\\alpha} scales as |b−p|/n|b-p|/\\\\sqrt{n}: bolder deviations from the market generate *more* signal about skill, but also more noise.
